1.

The petitioner has filed this petition under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. challenging the FIR No.
627/2015 registered at Police Station Mungeli, District Mungeli (C.G.) on 23.12.2015 for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 420 of the IPC.

sentences.text:
Facts of the present case are that, one Ganesh Dewangan lodged a report to the effect that the petitioner executed an agreement to sell in favour of the complainant with respect to land bearing survey No.627/3 admeasuring 0.25 acre, situated at Mungeli, Pa. Ha. No. 6, R.I. Circle Mungeli,
District Mungeli for consideration of Rs. 10,00,000/- and Rs. 8,00,100/- was given in advance.

It is further stated that Smt. Bela Singh and the petitioner were aware of the fact that the actual survey number of the plot is 627/2 even then they sold the property bearing incorrect survey No.627/3 to the complainant.
On such complaint police registered the offence as stated above.
It is stated by learned Counsel for the petitioner that the petitioner purchased the plot bearing survey No. 627/3 admeasuring 0.25 acre from one Bela Singh on 5.10.2012.
In the revenue records name of the petitioner was entered, thereafter he sold that plot to the complainant through a registered sale deed on 11.11.2013.

When the original owner, i.e., Smt. Bela Singh came across the fact that correct survey number of the plot is 627/2 and not 627/3, she moved an application for correction of the revenue records before the Tehsildar on 5.10.2015.

A report was called from the revenue inspector who submitted the report on 10.06.2016, wherein he categorically stated that survey No.627/2 total area 0.40 acre was recorded in the name of Ganesh Prasad who sold a plot of 4000 s.f. to Gurjeet Singh on 20.10.1989 and that plot was recorded as survey No. 627/3 in the revenue records.

It is further stated in the report that in the name of Ganesh Prasad survey No. 627/2 admeasuring 0.25 acre was recorded, due to clerical mistake in the sale deed dated 18.05.1992 instead of 627/2, survey No.627/3 was mentioned and this can be rectified.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner would further submit that from a careful reading of the above stated facts it is apparent that the mistake was bonafide and even in the sale deed survey No.627/3 was recorded and he executed the sale deed of the same land without knowing the fact that survey No.627/3 is recorded in the name of Gurjeet Singh.

He would pray to allow the petition.
4.

On the other hand, learned Counsel for the State and learned Counsel for the complainant would submit that the petitioner as well as Bela Singh were aware of the fact that correct servey number of the plot is 627/2 even then the petitioner executed the sale deed of survey No.627/3 knowing very well that said plot is recorded in the name of Gurjeet Singh.
They would further submit that area of survey No.627/2 and 627/3 are different.
They would argue that the petition deserves to be dismissed.
5. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the documents.

6. Section 415 of the IPC reads as Under:-
"415. Cheating.--Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat"."

sentences.text: In the matter of Vijay Kumar Ghai and Others Vs. State of West Bengal and Others, reported in AIR OnLine 2022 SC 380, it was observed that except for the allegations that on account of the act of cheating the complainant had suffered a wrongful loss and the same resulted in a wrongful gain for the accused, there was no intention on the part of the petitioner and/or others to cheat and/or to defraud the complainant right from the inception, therefore, the offences punishable under Section 420 of IPC would not be made out.

entities.text: Vijay Kumar Ghai and Others Vs. State of West Bengal and Others, reported in AIR OnLine 2022 SC 380
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The relevant paragraphs 33, 35 and 36 are reproduced herein below:

"33. The following observation made by this Court in the case of Uma Shankar Gopalika Vs. State of Bihar & Anr. 25 with almost similar facts and circumstances may be relevant to note at this stage:-
"6.

entities.text: Uma Shankar Gopalika Vs. State of Bihar & Anr. 25
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Now the question to be examined by us is as to whether on the facts disclosed in the petition of the complaint any criminal offence whatsoever is made out much less offences under Section 420/120-B IPC.

The only allegation in the complaint petitioner against the accused person is that they assured the complainant that when they receive the insurance claim amounting to Rs. 4,20,000, they would pay a sum of Rs. 2,60,000 to the complainant out of that but the same has never been paid.

It was pointed out that on behalf of the complainant that the accused fraudulently persuaded the complainant to agree so that the accused persons may take steps for moving the consumer forum in relation to the claim of Rs. 4,20,0000.

It is well settled that every breach of contract would not give rise to an offence of cheating and only in those cases of breach of contract would amount to cheating where there was any deception played at the very inception.
If the intention to cheat has developed later on, the same cannot amount to cheating.

In the present case, it has nowhere been stated that at the very inception that there was intention on behalf of the accused person to cheat which is a condition precedent for an offence under 420 IPC.

"7. In our view petition of complaint does not disclose any criminal offence at all much less any offence either under Section 420 or Section 120-B IPC and the present case is a case of purely civil dispute between the parties for which remedy lies before a civil court by filing a properly constituted suit.

In our opinion, in view of these facts allowing the police investigation to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of court and to prevent the same it was just and expedient for the High Court to quash the same by exercising the powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C which it has erroneously refused."
35. In Vesa Holdings Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. Vs. State of Kerala & Ors.

this Court made the following observation:-
"13.

It is true that a given set of facts may make out a civil wrong as also a criminal offence and only because a civil remedy may be available to the complainant that itself cannot be ground to quash a criminal proceeding.
The real test is whether the allegations in the complaint disclose the criminal offence of cheating or not.

sentences.text: Criminal proceedings should not be encouraged when it is found to be mala fide or otherwise an abuse of the process of the courts.
Superior courts while exercising this power should also strive to serve the ends of justice.

In our opinion, in view of these facts allowing the police investigation to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of the court and the High Court committed an error in refusing to exercise the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C to quash the proceedings."

Having gone through the complaint/FIR and even the chargesheet, it cannot be said that the averments in the FIR and the allegations in the complaint against the appellant constitute an offence under Section 405 & 420 IPC, 1860.

Even in a case where allegations are made in regard to failure on the part of the accused to keep his promise, in the absence of a culpable intention at the time of making promise being absent, no offence under Section 420 IPC can be said to have been made out.

In the instant case, there is no material to indicate that Appellants had any malafide intention against the Respondent which is clearly deductible from the MOU dated 20.08.2009 arrived between the parties.
36. Thus, we are of the considered view that the finding returned by the High Court suffers from an error of law.
It has delved into the field of appreciation and evaluation of the evidence which is beyond the jurisdiction, either revisional or inherent, of the High Court under Sections 397 and 482 of the Code."

In the matter of Vesa Holdings Private Limited Vs. State of Kerala and Others reported in (2015) 8 SCC 293 the Hon'ble Supreme Court while dealing with the ingredients of Section 420 of the IPC in paragraphs 12 & 13 held as under:
"12.

entities.text: Vesa Holdings Private Limited Vs. State of Kerala and Others reported in (2015) 8 SCC 293
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: From the decisions cited by the appellant, the settled proposition of law is that every breach of contract would not give rise to an offence of cheating and only in those cases breach of contract would amount to cheating where there was any deception played at the very inception.
If the intention to cheat has developed later on, the same cannot amount to cheating.

In other words for the purpose of constituting an offence of cheating, the complainant is required to show that the accused had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making promise or representation.

Even in a case where allegations are made in regard to failure on the part of the accused to keep his promise, in the absence of a culpable intention at the time of making initial promise being absent, no offence under Section 420 of the Penal Code, 1860 can be said to have been made out.

13. It is true that a given set of facts may make out a civil wrong as also a criminal offence and only because a civil remedy may be available to the complainant that itself cannot be a ground to quash a criminal proceeding.
The real test is whether the allegations in the complaint disclose the criminal offence of cheating or not.

sentences.text: In our view the complaint does not disclose any criminal offence at all.
The criminal proceedings should not be encouraged when it is found to be mala fide or otherwise an abuse of the process of the court.
The superior courts while exercising this power should also strive to serve the ends of justice.

In our opinion, in view of these facts allowing the police investigation to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of the court and the High Court committed an error in refusing to exercise the power under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash the proceedings."

In the matter of Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah Vs. State of Gujarat and Another, reported in AIR 2019 SC 1538, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that a mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless the fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction that is the time when the offence is said to have been committed.

entities.text: Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah Vs. State of Gujarat and Another, reported in AIR 2019 SC 1538
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the matter of Wyeth Limited and Others Vs. State of Bihar and Another reported in AIR OnLine 2022 SCC 1408, the Hon'ble Supreme Court quashed the FIR on the ground that prima facie offence of cheating was not made out.

entities.text: Wyeth Limited and Others Vs. State of Bihar and Another reported in AIR OnLine 2022 SCC 1408
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was held in paragraph 15 as under:-
"15.

The contention of the learned senior counsel for respondent No.2 that the Court has to take note of the final report filed by the police along with the statement of witnesses, could have been accepted by us, if the whole thing had emanated from a First Information lodged with the police.
Respondent No.2 actually filed a private complaint under Section 200 Cr.P.C, which was referred by the Court under Section 156(3) to the police.

When this complaint itself disclosed nothing more than a commercial relationship which broke, it is not possible for respondent No.2 to enlarge the scope of his complaint by merely adding the language used in the text of the Indian Penal Code."

In the matter of Binod Kumar and Others Vs. State of Bihar and Another, reported in 2014 AIR SCW 6310, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held the mere fact that the appellants did not pay the money to the complainant does not amount to a criminal breach of trust.

entities.text: Binod Kumar and Others Vs. State of Bihar and Another, reported in 2014 AIR SCW 6310
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The relevant paragraphs 18 & 19 are quoted herein below:

"18. In the present case, looking at the allegations in the complaint on the face of it,
we find no allegations are made attracting the ingredients of Section 405 IPC.

Likewise, there are no allegations as to cheating or the dishonest intention of the appellants in retaining the money in order to have wrongful gain to themselves or causing wrongful loss to the complainant.

Excepting the bald allegations that the appellants did not make payment to the second respondent and that the appellants utilized the amounts either by themselves or for some other work, there is no iota of allegation as to the dishonest intention in misappropriating the property.

To make out a case of criminal breach of trust, it is not sufficient to show that money has been Pranjal Jain vs State Of Chhattisgarh And Others on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52655614/
5 retained by the appellants.

entities.text: Pranjal Jain vs State Of Chhattisgarh And Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It must also be shown that the appellants dishonestly disposed of the same in some way or dishonestly retained the same.
The mere fact that the appellants did not pay the money to the complainant does not amount to criminal breach of trust.
19. Even if all the allegations in the complaint taken at the face value are true, in our view, the basic essential ingredients of dishonest misappropriation and cheating are missing.
Criminal proceedings are not a short cut for other remedies.

Since no case of criminal breach of trust or dishonest intention of inducement is made out and the essential ingredients of Sections 405/420 IPC are missing, the prosecution of the appellants under Sections 406/120B IPC, is liable to be quashed."

With regard to the inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 of Cr.P.C., the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of State of Haryana and Others Vs. Bhajan Lal and Others, reported in 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, in paragraph 103 held as under:
"103.

entities.text: State of Haryana and Others Vs. Bhajan Lal and Others, reported in 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We also give a note of caution to the effect that the power of quashing a criminal proceeding should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection and that too in the rarest of rare cases; that the court will not be justified in embarking upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness or otherwise of the allegations made in the FIR or the complaint and that the extraordinary or inherent powers do not confer an arbitrary jurisdiction on the court to act according to its whim or caprice."

In the matter of Amit Kapoor Vs. Ramesh Chander and Another, reported in (2012) 9 SCC 460,
framing of the charge has been discussed and it is held that if in the opinion of the Court, there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offence, it shall frame the charge.

entities.text: Amit Kapoor Vs. Ramesh Chander and Another, reported in (2012) 9 SCC 460
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 8. Now, coming to facts of the present case in light of the judgments rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court it is quite vivid that the petitioner purchased a plot bearing survey No.627/3 from Smt. Bela Singh through a registered sale deed dated 05.10.2012.
Thereafter, the same was sold to the complainant.
The fact of incorrect survey number was not within the knowledge of the petitioner and bonafidely he transferred the plot to the complainant.
To establish the ingredients of cheating there must be ill intention of an accused from very inception to cheat any person.
In the present case there is no material to show that the petitioner deliberately and knowingly sold the property with the knowledge that he is not the owner of survey No. 627/3.
Further, an application was moved by Smt. Bela Singh before the Tahsildar for correction of the revenue records when the fact of incorrect survey number surfaced.

The petitioner has purchased the plot on 05.10.2012 and sold it on 11.11.2013, whereas, the application before the Tahsildar was moved by Smt. Bela Singh on 05.10.2015 and thereafter, the complainant lodged the FIR on 23.12.2015.
The above stated facts would show that Smt. Bela Singh, the petitioner and the complainant were not aware about the fact that incorrect survey number is mentioned in their sale deeds.

The ingredients as stated in the matter of Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah (supra) are not satisfied in the present case, therefore, FIR No.627/2015 for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 420 of the IPC registered Pranjal Jain vs State Of Chhattisgarh And Others on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52655614/
6 at Police Station Mungeli, District Mungeli is hereby quashed.
